compare_blocks.body:

compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
In a fictional cross-team review, either person might suggest a new option or listen without speaking. What each does depends in part on the meeting’s purpose, their role and what is already known.

Both types share a preference for directing attention and energy outward and for noticing patterns and possibilities. Those preferences do not establish who will be more talkative or more effective at chairing a meeting.

The difference sits in two preferences: ENTP more often measures a proposal by criteria that can be applied consistently (T), ENFJ more often brings people and values into the judgement (F); outward, ENFJ more often forms a decision and a structure first (J), ENTP more often keeps options and keeps taking information in (P). Both get used; the question is which gets reached for first.

### ENFJ and ENTP: two entry points on hearing "we can't build that"

In a fictional review, development estimates four weeks for a bulk export feature and operations wants it by the end of the month. Both reviewers receive the same estimate, customer commitments and decision authority.

Either reviewer could weigh how a smaller release would affect customers or apply the same cost and feasibility criteria to each option. Those questions illustrate T/F. Separately, either could propose a provisional plan or keep several plans open until more information arrives. That choice illustrates J/P.

The chair's duty, the goal of the meeting and the deadline all rewrite the picture. In a meeting whose goal is "the client needs an answer today", both types more often push to close; in one whose goal is "clarify a vague requirement", both more often take assumptions apart.

Keep the counterexamples. With a client in the room waiting to sign, an ENTP may also give a conclusion on the spot and leave the unresolved part for afterwards; when a plan means two weeks of overtime for someone, an ENFJ may also take it apart and keep asking, because the cost has to land somewhere identifiable first.

To observe this pair, check whether the goal and the chair's duty were the same, then look at which kind of evidence each cited. Which column of the minutes is full reflects what the meeting had to produce far more than it reflects type.

### ENFJ and ENTP: why Fe and Ti are shared while the seats move far

In the four-function notation used here, ENFJ is Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and ENTP is Ne–Ti–Fe–Si. Fe and Ti survive in both, but in exchanged seats: Fe from first to third, Ti from fourth to second; what gets replaced is Ni against Ne and Se against Si. That holds only inside this writing and is not a conclusion independent of the convention.

Both types are extraverted, so their outward-facing process is dominant. In type dynamics, ENFJ’s J points to an outward judging process, Fe. ENTP’s P points to an outward perceiving process, Ne. ENTP’s preferred judging process in the model is Ti, its auxiliary.

These positions describe processing emphasis, not what an individual does first. In type dynamics the J/P of these two extraverts points to the outward judging process Fe and the outward perceiving process Ne respectively; T/F distinguishes their judging preferences as F and T. Position does not predict speaking order, areas of strength, rapport or attraction.

Whether the third process is labelled introverted or extraverted differs across sources. In this writing ENFJ's third is Se and ENTP's third is Fe; these are third functions of two different types, not two ways of writing the same position, and what is disputed is the attitude of the third process. compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
Division of work follows task and authority, not type: whoever knows the constraints best raises the alternatives; the chair records the disagreement clearly; whoever holds decision authority decides. The scenes below are editorial fiction, used to show what two kinds of trade-off can look like.

### ENFJ and ENTP: a cross-team review — can four weeks become two

(Fictional scene) A bulk-export requirement: operations wants it live by month end, development says four weeks, testing needs another week of regression, support says three customers are already asking. Six people in the room, one hour.

In this fictional review, the same estimate and release options are open to both reviewers. Either can ask which customers would be affected by reducing scope and which option meets the agreed effort and dependency criteria. The team can then decide which parts to commit to and which to leave open.

The costs are clear on both sides: closing today gets work started, with the risk of cutting the wrong scope and coming back in two weeks; taking it apart may run into a second meeting, with the risk of still verifying at month end. A workable compromise compares under the same information: spend twenty minutes listing the tiers, let whoever has authority choose one, then write the items to verify into the minutes with a named owner, method and deadline. Who does which part depends on who knows the schedule and who is authorised, not on four letters.

To observe, have each write two columns after the meeting — decided today, and not yet decided but verifiable — and swap before the next one: do the items in the second column have an owner, a method and a deadline. An empty column may simply mean the meeting only had to produce one of the two.

### ENFJ and ENTP: a week before release, operations wants a small "while you're in there" feature

(Fictional scene) After the code freeze, operations asks for a small change: add one customer-tag column to the export. Development says the change is small but needs a regression pass.

Both face the same information: how many interfaces change, how long regression takes, whether the release needs an announcement, whether the commitment to customers includes this column, and who explains if it breaks. Rollback time is one constraint among several and does not settle the question on its own.

In this fictional scene, one approach looks at commitments: what was promised to customers, whether adding this squeezes out regression, who stands up to explain if something goes wrong. The other looks at cost and exception: whether configuration can route around it, whether that old bug gets fixed at the same time, and whether there is an exception-admission rule that can be applied consistently. Either type can combine both; which step gets taken depends on the division of work, authority and the information available.

Suppose rollback takes ten minutes, no announcement is needed, and three enterprise customers are explicitly waiting for this column: either type may agree to let it in. Suppose rollback needs an announcement and involves data migration: either may refuse. The difference shows up more in the reason — one cites the effect on people and commitments, the other whether the exception rule holds consistently. Counterexamples exist too: before a major sales event, an ENTP may refuse the change outright; with a customer willing to pay extra for the column, an ENFJ may still refuse to let it in.

### ENFJ and ENTP: a friend of nine years has not replied for three days

The same silence is hard to read between friends. This passage is editorial fiction, pointing at no one, used to illustrate the difference between observations and guesses.

In the fictional friendship example, a longtime friend has not replied for three days. One possibility is that the last message landed badly. Another is that the friend is busy or unavailable. Either person can consider all these possibilities. A delayed reply cannot establish motive or type.

Both approaches have blind spots: reviewing yourself easily reads another person's silence as your own fault and sinks deeper while waiting; listing possibilities easily misses "he is actually angry", so a joke lands worse. These are explanations that may occur in some people, not fixed reactions determined by type, and they cannot establish the other person's motive either.

Write three lines separately: known facts, such as who sent the last message on Wednesday, what it said, whether anything was unusual before; your own guesses, such as he is not replying because of me, he is busy, the phone is broken; low-pressure information you could confirm, such as whether he is travelling, whether a mutual friend knows how he is. Whether to make contact, and how, depends on your usual way of communicating and the current state of the relationship — not on how many guesses have been eliminated; a delayed reply is not a conclusion in itself.

compare_blocks.body:
The first misread takes ENTP's questioning for not caring about people. Pressing on a proposal in a meeting may come from treating it as something improvable, or simply from wanting the risk stated; the same person may also seek someone out privately afterwards. Motive has several explanations, and one question in a meeting cannot settle it.

The second takes ENFJ's management of atmosphere for an absence of position. They may have decided before the meeting which direction to push and spent their effort on getting it accepted rather than on arguing for it. But that is one possible explanation, not a route every ENFJ follows.

The third writes the difference as ability: ENTP is smarter, ENFJ is better with people. Taking an assumption apart and pushing to closure are two operations, and either missing can leave a meeting unfinished; which is worth more depends on what the meeting has to produce and where the cost lands.

The fourth takes E for sociable and N for full of ideas. E says attention and energy turn outward more often; N says material lands on pattern and possibility more often. Either type can stay silent for a whole meeting, and either can check detail very closely when needed.

body: Division of work follows task and authority, not type: whoever knows the constraints best raises the alternatives; the chair records the disagreement clearly; whoever holds decision authority decides. The scenes below are editorial fiction, used to show what two kinds of trade-off can look like.
### ENFJ and ENTP: a cross-team review — can four weeks become two

(Fictional scene) A bulk-export requirement: operations wants it live by month end, development says four weeks, testing needs another week of regression, support says three customers are already asking. Six people in the room, one hour.

In this fictional review, the same estimate and release options are open to both reviewers. Either can ask which customers would be affected by reducing scope and which option meets the agreed effort and dependency criteria. The team can then decide which parts to commit to and which to leave open.

The costs are clear on both sides: closing today gets work started, with the risk of cutting the wrong scope and coming back in two weeks; taking it apart may run into a second meeting, with the risk of still verifying at month end. A workable compromise compares under the same information: spend twenty minutes listing the tiers, let whoever has authority choose one, then write the items to verify into the minutes with a named owner, method and deadline. Who does which part depends on who knows the schedule and who is authorised, not on four letters.

To observe, have each write two columns after the meeting — decided today, and not yet decided but verifiable — and swap before the next one: do the items in the second column have an owner, a method and a deadline. An empty column may simply mean the meeting only had to produce one of the two.
### ENFJ and ENTP: a week before release, operations wants a small "while you're in there" feature
(Fictional scene) After the code freeze, operations asks for a small change: add one customer-tag column to the export. Development says the change is small but needs a regression pass.

Both face the same information: how many interfaces change, how long regression takes, whether the release needs an announcement, whether the commitment to customers includes this column, and who explains if it breaks. Rollback time is one constraint among several and does not settle the question on its own.

In this fictional scene, one approach looks at commitments: what was promised to customers, whether adding this squeezes out regression, who stands up to explain if something goes wrong. The other looks at cost and exception: whether configuration can route around it, whether that old bug gets fixed at the same time, and whether there is an exception-admission rule that can be applied consistently. Either type can combine both; which step gets taken depends on the division of work, authority and the information available.

Suppose rollback takes ten minutes, no announcement is needed, and three enterprise customers are explicitly waiting for this column: either type may agree to let it in. Suppose rollback needs an announcement and involves data migration: either may refuse. The difference shows up more in the reason — one cites the effect on people and commitments, the other whether the exception rule holds consistently. Counterexamples exist too: before a major sales event, an ENTP may refuse the change outright; with a customer willing to pay extra for the column, an ENFJ may still refuse to let it in.

The same silence is hard to read between friends. This passage is editorial fiction, pointing at no one, used to illustrate the difference between observations and guesses.

In the fictional friendship example, a longtime friend has not replied for three days. One possibility is that the last message landed badly. Another is that the friend is busy or unavailable. Either person can consider all these possibilities. A delayed reply cannot establish motive or type.

Both approaches have blind spots: reviewing yourself easily reads another person's silence as your own fault and sinks deeper while waiting; listing possibilities easily misses "he is actually angry", so a joke lands worse. - E (Extraversion): attention and energy turn more often toward other people and the situation outside, and recover more easily through outside interaction. That is direction, not social skill, and not talkativeness; either type can spend a whole meeting not wanting to speak.

- J/P: the ENFJ side more often forms a decision and a structure outward first; the ENTP side more often keeps options and keeps taking information in.

sections.title: Quick answer

body: In a fictional cross-team review, either person might suggest a new option or listen without speaking. What each does depends in part on the meeting’s purpose, their role and what is already known.

Both types share a preference for directing attention and energy outward and for noticing patterns and possibilities. Those preferences do not establish who will be more talkative or more effective at chairing a meeting.

The difference sits in two preferences: ENTP more often measures a proposal by criteria that can be applied consistently (T), ENFJ more often brings people and values into the judgement (F); outward, ENFJ more often forms a decision and a structure first (J), ENTP more often keeps options and keeps taking information in (P). Both get used; the question is which gets reached for first.
### ENFJ and ENTP: two entry points on hearing "we can't build that"

In a fictional review, development estimates four weeks for a bulk export feature and operations wants it by the end of the month. Both reviewers receive the same estimate, customer commitments and decision authority.

Either reviewer could weigh how a smaller release would affect customers or apply the same cost and feasibility criteria to each option. Those questions illustrate T/F. Separately, either could propose a provisional plan or keep several plans open until more information arrives. That choice illustrates J/P.

The chair's duty, the goal of the meeting and the deadline all rewrite the picture. In a meeting whose goal is "the client needs an answer today", both types more often push to close; in one whose goal is "clarify a vague requirement", both more often take assumptions apart.

Keep the counterexamples. With a client in the room waiting to sign, an ENTP may also give a conclusion on the spot and leave the unresolved part for afterwards; when a plan means two weeks of overtime for someone, an ENFJ may also take it apart and keep asking, because the cost has to land somewhere identifiable first.

To observe this pair, check whether the goal and the chair's duty were the same, then look at which kind of evidence each cited. Which column of the minutes is full reflects what the meeting had to produce far more than it reflects type.
### ENFJ and ENTP: why Fe and Ti are shared while the seats move far

In the four-function notation used here, ENFJ is Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and ENTP is Ne–Ti–Fe–Si. Fe and Ti survive in both, but in exchanged seats: Fe from first to third, Ti from fourth to second; what gets replaced is Ni against Ne and Se against Si. That holds only inside this writing and is not a conclusion independent of the convention.

Both types are extraverted, so their outward-facing process is dominant. In type dynamics, ENFJ’s J points to an outward judging process, Fe. ENTP’s P points to an outward perceiving process, Ne. ENTP’s preferred judging process in the model is Ti, its auxiliary.

These positions describe processing emphasis, not what an individual does first. In type dynamics the J/P of these two extraverts points to the outward judging process Fe and the outward perceiving process Ne respectively; T/F distinguishes their judging preferences as F and T. Position does not predict speaking order, areas of strength, rapport or attraction.

Whether the third process is labelled introverted or extraverted differs across sources. In this writing ENFJ's third is Se and ENTP's third is Fe; these are third functions of two different types, not two ways of writing the same position, and what is disputed is the attitude of the third process. When a different version turns up, check whether that table states its convention. Item-by-item explanation sits on the [ENFJ profile](/en/personality/enfj) and the [ENTP profile](/en/personality/entp).

body: Align the conditions: the same requirements document, the same deadline, the same attendees, the same chair. Both types can use both approaches; the table only states which kind of evidence tends to be taken first. If one is chairing and the other merely attending, duty will swamp both columns.

| The same item in the meeting | ENFJ: evidence likely to be attended to first | ENTP: evidence likely to be attended to first | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What to sound out before the meeting | Weigh what each option would mean for the people who will use or maintain it | Apply the same feasibility and maintenance criteria to every option | Standard of judgement, leaning T/F |
| Hearing "we can't build that" | Weigh the effect of the available adjustments on users and colleagues | Apply the same effort and dependency criteria to the available adjustments | Standard of judgement, leaning T/F |
| The same plausible alternative comes up near the end of the meeting | Agree on a provisional direction and set a time to revisit the alternative | Keep the current direction and the alternative open until the same evidence is reviewed | Approach to outward arrangements: J/P |
| Being asked for a position on the spot | Agree on a provisional next step that can be revised after the same checks | Keep feasible next steps open until the same checks are complete | Outward stance, leaning J/P |
| Both document the same unresolved delivery choice | Record a provisional plan and when it will be reviewed | Record two workable plans to keep open until the agreed checks are complete | Approach to outward arrangements: J/P |
| Both consider the same request to change a delivery date | Weigh how the change would affect the people relying on delivery | Apply the same criteria for schedule changes that the team uses on comparable projects | Decision criteria: T/F |

None of these rows is a scale of ability. An ENFJ who has chaired projects for years may take the estimate apart by process first; an ENTP attending for the first time and only wanting the meeting to end may want a conclusion first. The same person also changes approach with the information at hand, the authority granted and whether the client is in the room, so these rows cannot be used to classify anyone.

body: Division of work follows task and authority, not type: whoever knows the constraints best raises the alternatives; the chair records the disagreement clearly; whoever holds decision authority decides. The scenes below are editorial fiction, used to show what two kinds of trade-off can look like.
### ENFJ and ENTP: a cross-team review — can four weeks become two

(Fictional scene) A bulk-export requirement: operations wants it live by month end, development says four weeks, testing needs another week of regression, support says three customers are already asking. Six people in the room, one hour.

In this fictional review, the same estimate and release options are open to both reviewers. Either can ask which customers would be affected by reducing scope and which option meets the agreed effort and dependency criteria. The team can then decide which parts to commit to and which to leave open.

The costs are clear on both sides: closing today gets work started, with the risk of cutting the wrong scope and coming back in two weeks; taking it apart may run into a second meeting, with the risk of still verifying at month end. A workable compromise compares under the same information: spend twenty minutes listing the tiers, let whoever has authority choose one, then write the items to verify into the minutes with a named owner, method and deadline. Who does which part depends on who knows the schedule and who is authorised, not on four letters.

To observe, have each write two columns after the meeting — decided today, and not yet decided but verifiable — and swap before the next one: do the items in the second column have an owner, a method and a deadline. An empty column may simply mean the meeting only had to produce one of the two.
### ENFJ and ENTP: a week before release, operations wants a small "while you're in there" feature
(Fictional scene) After the code freeze, operations asks for a small change: add one customer-tag column to the export. Development says the change is small but needs a regression pass.

Both face the same information: how many interfaces change, how long regression takes, whether the release needs an announcement, whether the commitment to customers includes this column, and who explains if it breaks. Rollback time is one constraint among several and does not settle the question on its own.

In this fictional scene, one approach looks at commitments: what was promised to customers, whether adding this squeezes out regression, who stands up to explain if something goes wrong. The other looks at cost and exception: whether configuration can route around it, whether that old bug gets fixed at the same time, and whether there is an exception-admission rule that can be applied consistently. Either type can combine both; which step gets taken depends on the division of work, authority and the information available.

Suppose rollback takes ten minutes, no announcement is needed, and three enterprise customers are explicitly waiting for this column: either type may agree to let it in. Suppose rollback needs an announcement and involves data migration: either may refuse. The difference shows up more in the reason — one cites the effect on people and commitments, the other whether the exception rule holds consistently. Counterexamples exist too: before a major sales event, an ENTP may refuse the change outright; with a customer willing to pay extra for the column, an ENFJ may still refuse to let it in.
### ENFJ and ENTP: a friend of nine years has not replied for three days
The same silence is hard to read between friends. This passage is editorial fiction, pointing at no one, used to illustrate the difference between observations and guesses.

In the fictional friendship example, a longtime friend has not replied for three days. One possibility is that the last message landed badly. Another is that the friend is busy or unavailable. Either person can consider all these possibilities. A delayed reply cannot establish motive or type.

Both approaches have blind spots: reviewing yourself easily reads another person's silence as your own fault and sinks deeper while waiting; listing possibilities easily misses "he is actually angry", so a joke lands worse. These are explanations that may occur in some people, not fixed reactions determined by type, and they cannot establish the other person's motive either.

Write three lines separately: known facts, such as who sent the last message on Wednesday, what it said, whether anything was unusual before; your own guesses, such as he is not replying because of me, he is busy, the phone is broken; low-pressure information you could confirm, such as whether he is travelling, whether a mutual friend knows how he is. Whether to make contact, and how, depends on your usual way of communicating and the current state of the relationship — not on how many guesses have been eliminated; a delayed reply is not a conclusion in itself.

body: The first misread takes ENTP's questioning for not caring about people. Pressing on a proposal in a meeting may come from treating it as something improvable, or simply from wanting the risk stated; the same person may also seek someone out privately afterwards. Motive has several explanations, and one question in a meeting cannot settle it.

The second takes ENFJ's management of atmosphere for an absence of position. They may have decided before the meeting which direction to push and spent their effort on getting it accepted rather than on arguing for it. But that is one possible explanation, not a route every ENFJ follows.

The third writes the difference as ability: ENTP is smarter, ENFJ is better with people. Taking an assumption apart and pushing to closure are two operations, and either missing can leave a meeting unfinished; which is worth more depends on what the meeting has to produce and where the cost lands.

The fourth takes E for sociable and N for full of ideas. E says attention and energy turn outward more often; N says material lands on pattern and possibility more often. Either type can stay silent for a whole meeting, and either can check detail very closely when needed.

body: When two results differ, check the item bank, language version, scoring definition and answering reference first, then look at which scene you had in mind: yourself in a meeting, or yourself deciding privately. A team with a strong review culture can push questioning into a standard move; a team under delivery pressure can push closure into one — what gets measured may only be the habit of the post.

If the platform reports T/F and J/P dimension scores with classification thresholds, see whether both sittings sit near a threshold. Near-threshold only means the label is sensitive to changes in answering; it does not mean two complete types both hold. Without dimension scores or scoring notes, do not infer a near-boundary result. When comparing two sittings, keep the item version, language and reference as consistent as possible rather than retesting in a different scene and calling it verification.

The practice can take a few recent events — a review, a scheduling negotiation, a discussion at home about changing a plan — and record a few lines for each: what information was trusted, what standard was used to weigh it, who had authority, how tight the deadline was, and which condition, if changed, would have changed your approach. If "does the standard hold consistently", "what this means for the people involved" or "settle it now or look again" keeps recurring, that is worth discussing as your habits of gathering and judging. These notes serve reflection, are not scored, do not assign a type, and cannot be replaced by inferring type from what someone says in a meeting.

body: **Framework sources** The four preference definitions follow the [Myers-Briggs official facts page](https://www.themyersbriggs.com/en-us/support/mbti-facts). The type-dynamics framework follows the Foundation's [note on type dynamics](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-processes/) and the [type dynamics overview](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/): the first sets out the eight processes and the basic assumptions of type dynamics, the second gives the common arrangement for each type.

**Four-position convention on this page** The Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and Ne–Ti–Fe–Si written here, in particular the attitude of the third process, follow one common four-function notation adopted here as an editorial convention. Other sources label the third process differently; this page does not present the writing as the Foundation's only reading, nor infer behaviour order, areas of strength, rapport or attraction from it.

**Editorial fiction note** The cross-team requirements review, the post-freeze feature request and the friend's three days of silence are all editorial fiction, corresponding to no real person, team or event, and are used only to illustrate possible trade-offs. The scenes are not for typing; one or several behavioural observations cannot be converted directly into a type.

**Scope limits** This page discusses emphasis between preferences, not a scale of ability, and it does not establish anyone's motive. Results are not for ranking ability, hiring screens or predicting relationships; situations involving medical care, emergency response or psychological crisis belong to qualified professionals. sections.body_md:
ENFJ and ENTP share Extraversion (E) and Intuition (N). They differ in how they tend to weigh decisions (T/F) and whether they prefer to settle arrangements or keep options open in the outside world (J/P).

- E (Extraversion): attention and energy turn more often toward other people and the situation outside, and recover more easily through outside interaction. That is direction, not social skill, and not talkativeness; either type can spend a whole meeting not wanting to speak.
- N (Intuition): information lands first on patterns, connections and possibility rather than on observable facts checked one by one. Either type can be exacting about detail; the entry point is more often "what could this mean".
- T/F: the ENTP side more often judges by impersonal criteria that can be applied consistently; the ENFJ side more often puts people and values into the judgement.
- J/P: the ENFJ side more often forms a decision and a structure outward first; the ENTP side more often keeps options and keeps taking information in.

In the notation used here, ENFJ is Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and ENTP is Ne–Ti–Fe–Si. Fe is dominant for ENFJ and third for ENTP. Ti is fourth for ENFJ and auxiliary for ENTP. The perceiving functions differ, and sources vary in how they label the third process.

These preferences describe emphasis inside the model. They do not order behaviour, and they do not predict who speaks first or who makes the call. sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
In a fictional cross-team review, either person might suggest a new option or listen without speaking. What each does depends in part on the meeting’s purpose, their role and what is already known.

Both types share a preference for directing attention and energy outward and for noticing patterns and possibilities. Those preferences do not establish who will be more talkative or more effective at chairing a meeting.

The difference sits in two preferences: ENTP more often measures a proposal by criteria that can be applied consistently (T), ENFJ more often brings people and values into the judgement (F); outward, ENFJ more often forms a decision and a structure first (J), ENTP more often keeps options and keeps taking information in (P). Both get used; the question is which gets reached for first.

### ENFJ and ENTP: two entry points on hearing "we can't build that"

In a fictional review, development estimates four weeks for a bulk export feature and operations wants it by the end of the month. Both reviewers receive the same estimate, customer commitments and decision authority.

Either reviewer could weigh how a smaller release would affect customers or apply the same cost and feasibility criteria to each option. Those questions illustrate T/F. Separately, either could propose a provisional plan or keep several plans open until more information arrives. That choice illustrates J/P.

The chair's duty, the goal of the meeting and the deadline all rewrite the picture. In a meeting whose goal is "the client needs an answer today", both types more often push to close; in one whose goal is "clarify a vague requirement", both more often take assumptions apart.

Keep the counterexamples. With a client in the room waiting to sign, an ENTP may also give a conclusion on the spot and leave the unresolved part for afterwards; when a plan means two weeks of overtime for someone, an ENFJ may also take it apart and keep asking, because the cost has to land somewhere identifiable first.

To observe this pair, check whether the goal and the chair's duty were the same, then look at which kind of evidence each cited. Which column of the minutes is full reflects what the meeting had to produce far more than it reflects type.

### ENFJ and ENTP: why Fe and Ti are shared while the seats move far

In the four-function notation used here, ENFJ is Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and ENTP is Ne–Ti–Fe–Si. Fe and Ti survive in both, but in exchanged seats: Fe from first to third, Ti from fourth to second; what gets replaced is Ni against Ne and Se against Si. That holds only inside this writing and is not a conclusion independent of the convention.

Both types are extraverted, so their outward-facing process is dominant. In type dynamics, ENFJ’s J points to an outward judging process, Fe. ENTP’s P points to an outward perceiving process, Ne. ENTP’s preferred judging process in the model is Ti, its auxiliary.

These positions describe processing emphasis, not what an individual does first. In type dynamics the J/P of these two extraverts points to the outward judging process Fe and the outward perceiving process Ne respectively; T/F distinguishes their judging preferences as F and T. Position does not predict speaking order, areas of strength, rapport or attraction.

Whether the third process is labelled introverted or extraverted differs across sources. In this writing ENFJ's third is Se and ENTP's third is Fe; these are third functions of two different types, not two ways of writing the same position, and what is disputed is the attitude of the third process. When a different version turns up, check whether that table states its convention. Item-by-item explanation sits on the [ENFJ profile](/en/personality/enfj) and the [ENTP profile](/en/personality/entp).

sections.body_md:
Align the conditions: the same requirements document, the same deadline, the same attendees, the same chair. Both types can use both approaches; the table only states which kind of evidence tends to be taken first. If one is chairing and the other merely attending, duty will swamp both columns.

| The same item in the meeting | ENFJ: evidence likely to be attended to first | ENTP: evidence likely to be attended to first | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What to sound out before the meeting | Weigh what each option would mean for the people who will use or maintain it | Apply the same feasibility and maintenance criteria to every option | Standard of judgement, leaning T/F |
| Hearing "we can't build that" | Weigh the effect of the available adjustments on users and colleagues | Apply the same effort and dependency criteria to the available adjustments | Standard of judgement, leaning T/F |
| The same plausible alternative comes up near the end of the meeting | Agree on a provisional direction and set a time to revisit the alternative | Keep the current direction and the alternative open until the same evidence is reviewed | Approach to outward arrangements: J/P |
| Being asked for a position on the spot | Agree on a provisional next step that can be revised after the same checks | Keep feasible next steps open until the same checks are complete | Outward stance, leaning J/P |
| Both document the same unresolved delivery choice | Record a provisional plan and when it will be reviewed | Record two workable plans to keep open until the agreed checks are complete | Approach to outward arrangements: J/P |
| Both consider the same request to change a delivery date | Weigh how the change would affect the people relying on delivery | Apply the same criteria for schedule changes that the team uses on comparable projects | Decision criteria: T/F |

None of these rows is a scale of ability. An ENFJ who has chaired projects for years may take the estimate apart by process first; an ENTP attending for the first time and only wanting the meeting to end may want a conclusion first. The same person also changes approach with the information at hand, the authority granted and whether the client is in the room, so these rows cannot be used to classify anyone.
sections.title: ENFJ and ENTP in one minute

sections.body_md:
Division of work follows task and authority, not type: whoever knows the constraints best raises the alternatives; the chair records the disagreement clearly; whoever holds decision authority decides. The scenes below are editorial fiction, used to show what two kinds of trade-off can look like.

### ENFJ and ENTP: a cross-team review — can four weeks become two

(Fictional scene) A bulk-export requirement: operations wants it live by month end, development says four weeks, testing needs another week of regression, support says three customers are already asking. Six people in the room, one hour.

In this fictional review, the same estimate and release options are open to both reviewers. Either can ask which customers would be affected by reducing scope and which option meets the agreed effort and dependency criteria. The team can then decide which parts to commit to and which to leave open.

The costs are clear on both sides: closing today gets work started, with the risk of cutting the wrong scope and coming back in two weeks; taking it apart may run into a second meeting, with the risk of still verifying at month end. A workable compromise compares under the same information: spend twenty minutes listing the tiers, let whoever has authority choose one, then write the items to verify into the minutes with a named owner, method and deadline. Who does which part depends on who knows the schedule and who is authorised, not on four letters.

To observe, have each write two columns after the meeting — decided today, and not yet decided but verifiable — and swap before the next one: do the items in the second column have an owner, a method and a deadline. An empty column may simply mean the meeting only had to produce one of the two.

### ENFJ and ENTP: a week before release, operations wants a small "while you're in there" feature

(Fictional scene) After the code freeze, operations asks for a small change: add one customer-tag column to the export. Development says the change is small but needs a regression pass.

Both face the same information: how many interfaces change, how long regression takes, whether the release needs an announcement, whether the commitment to customers includes this column, and who explains if it breaks. Rollback time is one constraint among several and does not settle the question on its own.

In this fictional scene, one approach looks at commitments: what was promised to customers, whether adding this squeezes out regression, who stands up to explain if something goes wrong. The other looks at cost and exception: whether configuration can route around it, whether that old bug gets fixed at the same time, and whether there is an exception-admission rule that can be applied consistently. Either type can combine both; which step gets taken depends on the division of work, authority and the information available.

Suppose rollback takes ten minutes, no announcement is needed, and three enterprise customers are explicitly waiting for this column: either type may agree to let it in. Suppose rollback needs an announcement and involves data migration: either may refuse. The difference shows up more in the reason — one cites the effect on people and commitments, the other whether the exception rule holds consistently. Counterexamples exist too: before a major sales event, an ENTP may refuse the change outright; with a customer willing to pay extra for the column, an ENFJ may still refuse to let it in.

### ENFJ and ENTP: a friend of nine years has not replied for three days

The same silence is hard to read between friends. This passage is editorial fiction, pointing at no one, used to illustrate the difference between observations and guesses.

In the fictional friendship example, a longtime friend has not replied for three days. One possibility is that the last message landed badly. Another is that the friend is busy or unavailable. Either person can consider all these possibilities. A delayed reply cannot establish motive or type.

Both approaches have blind spots: reviewing yourself easily reads another person's silence as your own fault and sinks deeper while waiting; listing possibilities easily misses "he is actually angry", so a joke lands worse. These are explanations that may occur in some people, not fixed reactions determined by type, and they cannot establish the other person's motive either.

Write three lines separately: known facts, such as who sent the last message on Wednesday, what it said, whether anything was unusual before; your own guesses, such as he is not replying because of me, he is busy, the phone is broken; low-pressure information you could confirm, such as whether he is travelling, whether a mutual friend knows how he is. Whether to make contact, and how, depends on your usual way of communicating and the current state of the relationship — not on how many guesses have been eliminated; a delayed reply is not a conclusion in itself.

sections.body_md:
The first misread takes ENTP's questioning for not caring about people. Pressing on a proposal in a meeting may come from treating it as something improvable, or simply from wanting the risk stated; the same person may also seek someone out privately afterwards. Motive has several explanations, and one question in a meeting cannot settle it.

The second takes ENFJ's management of atmosphere for an absence of position. They may have decided before the meeting which direction to push and spent their effort on getting it accepted rather than on arguing for it. But that is one possible explanation, not a route every ENFJ follows.

The third writes the difference as ability: ENTP is smarter, ENFJ is better with people. Taking an assumption apart and pushing to closure are two operations, and either missing can leave a meeting unfinished; which is worth more depends on what the meeting has to produce and where the cost lands.

The fourth takes E for sociable and N for full of ideas. E says attention and energy turn outward more often; N says material lands on pattern and possibility more often. Either type can stay silent for a whole meeting, and either can check detail very closely when needed.

sections.body_md:
When two results differ, check the item bank, language version, scoring definition and answering reference first, then look at which scene you had in mind: yourself in a meeting, or yourself deciding privately. A team with a strong review culture can push questioning into a standard move; a team under delivery pressure can push closure into one — what gets measured may only be the habit of the post.

If the platform reports T/F and J/P dimension scores with classification thresholds, see whether both sittings sit near a threshold. Near-threshold only means the label is sensitive to changes in answering; it does not mean two complete types both hold. Without dimension scores or scoring notes, do not infer a near-boundary result. When comparing two sittings, keep the item version, language and reference as consistent as possible rather than retesting in a different scene and calling it verification.

The practice can take a few recent events — a review, a scheduling negotiation, a discussion at home about changing a plan — and record a few lines for each: what information was trusted, what standard was used to weigh it, who had authority, how tight the deadline was, and which condition, if changed, would have changed your approach. If "does the standard hold consistently", "what this means for the people involved" or "settle it now or look again" keeps recurring, that is worth discussing as your habits of gathering and judging. These notes serve reflection, are not scored, do not assign a type, and cannot be replaced by inferring type from what someone says in a meeting.

items.answer:
T/F and J/P; E and N are shared.

T/F compares the standard of judgement: impersonal and consistently applicable, or people and values brought in. J/P compares the outward stance: a decision and structure first, or options kept while more information comes in. Both types use both approaches in both places, and order is not a test; what discriminates better is which kind of evidence recurs across comparable situations.
items.question: Which two preferences hold the difference?

items.answer:
In the four-function notation used here, ENFJ is Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and ENTP is Ne–Ti–Fe–Si. Fe and Ti remain on both sides, while Ni against Ne and Se against Si are replaced.

Under this convention, the outward-facing process leads in both extraverted types. ENFJ’s J points to Fe, a judging process. ENTP’s P points to Ne, a perceiving process, while Ti is its auxiliary judging process. Fe and Ti therefore appear in both stacks in different positions. The third-process label varies by source.
items.question: Why do the two stacks share only two functions?

items.answer:
They can, but not from a single behaviour, and not from who says what first.

What discriminates better is the reason: across comparable situations, do you more often cite whether this standard applies consistently and where the estimate comes from, or what this means for the people involved and who should be included. Whether the care happens in the meeting or afterwards, and whether the argument targets the proposal or the person, depends more on the setting, the relationship and the risk at that moment; one performance cannot establish motive.
items.question: An ENTP also looks after people's feelings, an ENFJ also argues — can they still be told apart?

items.answer:
Not a question of type, but of what the meeting has to produce, who knows the constraints and who holds authority.

If a decision is needed today, set the agenda to present tiers, converge, and have owners claim items on the spot; if a vague requirement needs clarifying, set it to list assumptions, mark verification methods and deadlines. Either type can chair either agenda; whoever knows the schedule is better placed to reconcile estimate disputes, and whoever holds decision authority is better placed to decide — none of which relates to four letters.
items.question: Which is better suited to chairing a requirements review?

items.answer:
Usually on what counts as a finished meeting: one feels that no owner means no meeting, the other feels that fixing an owner before verification plants a problem.

A workable agreement leaves two columns in every meeting — decided items with owner and date, undecided items with verifier, method and deadline; fill them only when there are items, mark "none" when there are not, and never invent entries to fill the space. Whoever chairs uses the same sheet, and the two kinds of output can also be split across two meetings.
items.question: Working on a project together, where do they most often jam?

items.answer:
Two different results cannot establish whether your preferences changed.

Check the questionnaire, language and scoring guide. If the tool reports comparable T/F and J/P scores and explains the cutoffs, check how close each result was to its cutoff. Workplace responsibilities can influence which examples you think of when answering. Compare several situations in which you had room to choose.

**Framework sources** The four preference definitions follow the [Myers-Briggs official facts page](https://www.themyersbriggs.com/en-us/support/mbti-facts). The type-dynamics framework follows the Foundation's [note on type dynamics](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-processes/) and the [type dynamics overview](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/): the first sets out the eight processes and the basic assumptions of type dynamics, the second gives the common arrangement for each type.

**Four-position convention on this page** The Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and Ne–Ti–Fe–Si written here, in particular the attitude of the third process, follow one common four-function notation adopted here as an editorial convention. Other sources label the third process differently; this page does not present the writing as the Foundation's only reading, nor infer behaviour order, areas of strength, rapport or attraction from it.

**Editorial fiction note** The cross-team requirements review, the post-freeze feature request and the friend's three days of silence are all editorial fiction, corresponding to no real person, team or event, and are used only to illustrate possible trade-offs. The scenes are not for typing; one or several behavioural observations cannot be converted directly into a type.

**Scope limits** This page discusses emphasis between preferences, not a scale of ability, and it does not establish anyone's motive. Results are not for ranking ability, hiring screens or predicting relationships; situations involving medical care, emergency response or psychological crisis belong to qualified professionals. The FermatMind assessment uses its own item bank and scoring, described in the [scoring and evidence note](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).
